runs.text: P. Sombra de mõte de mui-

lines.note: Miyamagacure denotes shade or concealment in a thickly wooded mountain, marked poetic by P. The scan has a nasal tilde in mõte, not the OCR's grave accent; mui- continues onto the next row.
To completes muito, describing abundant woodland. This continuation is visibly indented rather than aligned with the headword as in the provisional markup.
Miyamajitoto is cross-referred to the bird-name entry Miyama on f0324. Vide is italic editorial Latin, while both Japanese names remain upright.
Miyari means casting one's eyes in a direction. The past form atta is actually printed; the Portuguese divides alguma after al-.
Completes the direction of the glance as some place or other. This short phrase belongs to Miyari, not to the following royal title.
Miyasudokoro is explained as a queen who already has a child. The next physical row specifies the child's princely status.
Principe completes filho principe. The dictionary's status-specific definition is retained without replacing it with a broader modern account of the title.

runs.text: Seruiço feito a peſſoa nobre. Vt,

lines.note: Miyazukai is service rendered to a noble person. The scan shows two long-s types in peſſoa here, unlike the ligature-like form in nearby occurrences.
Miyazukai no nyoobootachi denotes the women engaged in such service. The two long-o marks in nhôbǒtachi are different: circumflex first, caron second.

runs.text: ſeruem a peßoa nobre principalmente a Cũgues.

lines.note: The women serve noble people, especially court nobles. Cũgues is the pluralized Japanese title embedded in Portuguese; the tilde over u is retained.
The verbal Miyazzucai means serving a noble person. The supplied long-o principal parts carry carons and are not converted to modern conjugation forms.
The service is especially to court nobles, completing the verb's gloss. The lower-case cũgues differs in capitalization from the preceding example and is preserved.
Miye covers becoming visible or appearing, as well as seeming. The Portuguese pairs aparecer and parecer rather than restricting the entry to physical sight alone.
Miyekitari is appearing or arriving from outside. The visible initial f of fo- and the continuation ra establish fora, not the OCR's ſora.
Miyekitari-soro aida xinji-soro means offering something because it has arrived. The scan supports xinjiſoro, the giving/offering expression, not the OCR's malformed ximiſoro.

runs.text: Ofereço vos isto por me vir agora de fora.

lines.note: The speaker offers the object because it has just come from elsewhere. This confirms the offering verb in the Japanese example rather than treating it as an unrelated action.
Miyesome is beginning to appear. The entry is a compound with the beginning-of-action element some, directly matched by começar.
Miyewatari is being visible far away or across an entire extent. The final lõ- begins the Portuguese longe on the next row.
The gloss adds visibility along the whole length, then begins a quotation about a great distance. Farucani to- continues into tooki on the next row.
The remote limits of mountains and sea are said to be hazy. Kasumitaredomo supplies the concessive sense, although they are obscured by haze.
Everything is nevertheless visible before the honored eyes. The scan has a nasal tilde in võmeno, not a long-vowel caron; interpreting it as onme no avoids the stale hint's oome reading.
Nari closes the Japanese statement. Chr. N. is retained as the printed upright citation label without conjectural expansion; Lib. 8 and the translation are italic.

runs.text: nos do mar, & dos montes muito distantes que

lines.note: The translation names the very distant limits of the sea and mountains. Nos completes terminos from the preceding row.

runs.text: eſtauão ẽneuoados, todauia aparecerão todos cla-

lines.note: Those distant places were shrouded in mist but nevertheless appeared clearly. The printed ẽneuoados is one word, with an abbreviation tilde, not the OCR's separated ẽ neuoados.
Ramente completes claramente, closing the translation of the long-distance-visibility quotation. It is a genuine short continuation.

runs.text: Parte direita do falcão, que he aparte,

lines.note: Miyori names the falcon's right side in the handling position described below. The gloss anchors the terminology in falconry rather than in the ordinary sense of family connections.

runs.text: ou aſas que ficão vizinhas ao corpo do homem

lines.note: This is the side or wings nearest the handler's body. The relative orientation is completed by the description of the arm carrying the bird.

runs.text: que o tem no braço eſquerdo.

lines.note: The bird is held on the left arm; Tadaſaqi then introduces the contrasting side. The Japanese label is part of the explanatory comparison, followed by Portuguese He.
Tadasaki is the left side or left wings in this comparison. The printed plural aſas is retained rather than anatomically regularized.
The poetic Miyuki means deep snow, explained by fukai yuki. P. is upright in this occurrence; it is a usage label, not an italic fragment of the headword.
Da completes amontoada, snow piled up or lying high. This closes the snow entry before the distinct royal-travel entry.
A separate Miyuki means the ruler's going out or journey. It begins at the headword margin, not at continuation indentation.

runs.text: O ver algũa couſa friamente, ou ſẽ

lines.note: Mizame describes regarding something coldly or without the earlier enthusiasm. The visible tilde in ſẽ supplies the negative preposition sem; it must not be dropped as in the OCR.

runs.text: aquelle feruor cõ q̃ primeiro a via. ¶

lines.note: The lost enthusiasm is that with which the thing was first regarded. Mizame begins the illustrative Japanese expression at the row end.
Mizame ga suru, or xita, describes that cooling of interest. The prose then identifies a regional equivalent used in Ximo; the printed final punctuation is a semicolon.
Misabita supplies that regional expression for the same cooling or loss of freshness in one's regard. The visible long s is preserved, not changed to f.
Mizao is the bamboo or pole used with a boat. The short definition identifies an implement, not the channel itself.

runs.text: Regato, ou cano que vai pello chão.

lines.note: Mizo is a ditch or channel running along the ground. Enlargement resolves the OCR's pll as pello, retaining the printed doubled l.
Mizogawa is a small stream or rivulet, extending mizo into a compound. The Portuguese smallness qualification is explicit.

runs.text: Neue que cae miſturada com chuua.

lines.note: Mizore is snow falling mixed with rain. The next paragraph applies this mixed appearance figuratively to a drink.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Certo vinho branco de Na

lines.note: The figurative extension is a particular white wine from Nara. Na continues into ra on the next physical row without an added hyphen.

runs.text: ra, que tem dentro miſturada a caſca do arroz.

lines.note: Ra completes Nara; the drink has rice husk mixed into it according to the gloss. The historical description is retained rather than replaced with a modern brewing explanation.
Mizosanzai is a small bird, with a cross-reference to Misosanzai. The voiced spelling of this headword and the unvoiced spelling in the reference are distinct as printed.
Completes Mi-ſoſanzai, the cross-referred bird name. This fragment is not a new headword or an embedded word in Portuguese prose.
Mizou is explained by imada katsute arazu, something that has never occurred before. The circumflex and following u are retained rather than condensed to a modern spelling.
Completes acontecida: not having happened up to now. The closing S. is upright and marks written usage.

Mizzu is water. Mizzuuo ſumaſu means making water clear, leading into A-clarar at the next column's opening; this restores the badly garbled headword, gloss, object particle, and verb without adding a new physical row.
Clarar completes A-clarar from the previous column, making the water clear. Mizzuni tçucaru then introduces immersing oneself in water; Me- begins its translation.
Terſe completes meterſe na agoa. Mizzuuo caquru is pouring or casting water on something, with Bo- belonging wholly to the italic Portuguese verb Botar.

runs.text: tar agoa em cima dalgũa couſa. ¶

lines.note: Tar completes Botar, specifically putting water on top of something. Mizzu- begins the next example and remains divided at this physical line boundary.
Mizzu-ga masu means the water rises, glossed as a river carrying a large flood. Enlargement supports the separate ga maſu, not the OCR's gaimaſu.
Mizzuuo cumu means drawing water. A new example, beginning Miz-, follows the paragraph mark and is completed on the next row.
Mizzuuo musubu is a poetic expression for taking water or washing. P. is visibly upright here and labels the Japanese usage before the italic explanation.
The washing concerns the face or hands. Mizzuuo sosogu introduces sprinkling water; the long-s forms in the Japanese verb are preserved.
The sprinkling gloss ends, then mizzuuo utsu begins an example of casting water. The Portuguese Botar leads into the house-or-courtyard explanation below.

runs.text: agoa como quẽ agoa a caſa, ou pateo.

lines.note: The water is spread as when watering a house or courtyard. The tilde in quẽ is retained rather than expanded to quem.
Mizubishaku is a water-drawing dipper, described as a coco. The Portuguese material term is not silently replaced with a modern utensil name.
Mizubune denotes a water basin or washing place. The gloss uses pia and lauatorio as explanatory alternatives.
Mizukane is mercury, glossed by azougue. The entry is a metal name despite its literal association with water and its position among mizzu forms.
Mizucara is the reflexive or emphatic myself, glossed Eu meſmo, not a water compound. The final upright S. marks written usage.
Mizukasa denotes a river's rising water or flood level. The following example describes an actual increase in that level.
Mizukaſaga maita describes the water level having risen, translated as a great flood arriving. The printed maita is retained as the historical form rather than changed to a modern -shita ending.
Chente completes enchente, a flood of water. This short continuation closes the mizukasa example.

runs.text: Vaſo em que deitão a agoa cõ

lines.note: Mizukoboshi is a vessel into which used water is poured. The following row specifies rinsing the porcelain used for tea.
The vessel receives the water used to rinse tea porcelain. Cha is embedded in the Portuguese gloss; S. is an upright usage label, and the printed aporſolana is not respelled.
Mizukoshi is a strainer for filtering water. The repeated Portuguese coador and coar expresses the implement and its function.

runs.text: Aguadeiro, ou o que tira agoa.

lines.note: Mizukumi denotes a water carrier or someone who draws water. This is the person performing the action, not another container.
Mizukuroi is arranging one's appearance, specifically straightening and tugging at clothing. This is body-grooming vocabulary, not a compound about repairing water.
The clothing is adjusted so that one is properly dressed. Tori ga mizzu- begins an analogous example concerning a bird's grooming.
The bird performs mizukuroi; fazzukuroi is supplied as the preferable expression. Meliùs is one italic editorial word, not a mixture of Japanese and Portuguese runs.
The Portuguese explains that the bird is preening itself. Ru completes the Japanese suru of the preferred wording from the preceding line.

runs.text: Barrijs de pao, ou tinas peque-

lines.note: Mizudaru first denotes wooden barrels or small water tubs. The list of vessel-related senses continues below.

runs.text: nas de agoa. ¶ Item, Tanque dagoa nas

lines.note: The first sense ends with water tubs; the next is a water tank in a vessel. Nas leads into embarcaçoens on the next row.
The second sense concerns boats, while a third is a container of wine. The following row qualifies that wine as unaccompanied by food.
Sem Sacana means without food accompanying the drink. The Japanese example begins by referring to even a single mizudaru.
The speaker says he has not received even that small courtesy or gift. The Portuguese begins the corresponding negative statement, Nem hũa bar-.

runs.text: ça de vinho ſò ſem Sacana medeu.

lines.note: Completes barça and explains that not even wine alone, without sakana, was given. Sacana is embedded in Portuguese, while the joined medeu preserves the printed spacing.
Mizuhajiki is a water-squirting device compared with a syringe. The alternative Japanese term is supplied on the following short row.
The upright Latin l introduces Mizzutçuqi as the alternative name. Neither the marker nor the Japanese word belongs to an italic Portuguese run.

runs.text: Certo genero de peixe como lin-

lines.note: Mizugare names a fish compared with a sole or flatfish. The comparison is explicit, but the brief gloss does not establish a precise modern species.
Guado completes linguado, the Portuguese comparator. The physical line break is preserved even though it divides a single word.
Mizugoromo is a garment of very thin silk. The following row specifies its use as an outer layer in theatrical performance.

runs.text: que ſe veſte por cima nos autos, &c.

lines.note: The thin garment is worn over other clothing in plays or performances. Autos is theatrical here, not a modern sense involving vehicles.
Mizuguchi denotes an opening from which water flows. The Portuguese boca is used for the outlet or mouth of the flow.
Mizuguki is glossed as a Japanese writing pen or brush. Pena is an explanatory instrument term here, not a statement that the object is necessarily a bird's feather.
Mizuguruma is a water-lifting wheel compared with a nora. The source from which it lifts water follows on the next row.
The wheel raises water from rivers or streams. This completes the mechanism's function rather than describing a water-driven mill.
Mizuzeme is torture by water. The example starts with the visibly spaced Mizz u-, retained from the print rather than silently closing the gap.
Jemeuo suru completes the Japanese example, applying water torture. The Portuguese gives the same action, and its joined Dartormento is retained.
Mizzuire is a very small vessel used to pour water. The destination, an ink container, is specified on the next row.
The water is poured into the inkwell or ink receptacle. This identifies the vessel's writing-related use without replacing the printed terminology.
Mizuiro denotes a light blue color. The Portuguese prints azulclaro together; that spelling is retained.
Mizumasagumo names small clouds; the shape and density are described on the next row. The entry starts at the headword margin, so the provisional indentation is removed.

runs.text: nas, & ralas, que aparecem como ondas.

lines.note: The clouds are thin and look like waves, completing the descriptive gloss. The signature and the catchword below are separate page furniture.

The small terminal mark is worn and nearly dot-shaped. It sits above the normal full-stop level; retain the dash reading Mizzu-, the divided-word cue for Mizzunaburi on the following page, rather than silently supplying a different catchword.
